---
title: "Spool"
sidebar: api
---

In the proposed workflow, DASCore's `Spool` acts as a bridge between stored patch (time-series) data and the DASDAE `Inventory`. The spool finds the relevant patches using indexed patch metadata; the selected patches then use `Inventory` for richer context querying, selectively transferring coordinates/metadata, etc.

## Inventory Workflow

### Spool operations

The inventory can be directly attached to a spool, in which case it acts as a metadata-fallback for patch operations. 

```python
import dascore as dc

inventory = dc.inventory("inventory.yaml")

# Attaching resolves every indexed patch against the inventory and
# updates the index to match; unresolvable patches raise by default.
spool = dc.spool("/data/archive").attach_inventory(inventory)


raw = (
    spool
    # Get rid of channels with undefined coupling
    .unselect(coupling=None)
    # Coordinate selection from corresponding coordinates
    .select(latitude=(45, 50), elevation=(100, 250))
)

patch = raw[0]
```

`attach_inventory` applies an `on_missing` policy to patches that resolve to no inventory entry — a `data_source_id` the inventory does not contain, or a time outside every matching epoch. The default is `"raise"`, which fails immediately and names the unmatched IDs; `"warn"` drops them but reports what was dropped; `"drop"` discards them silently, the right choice only when the inventory intentionally covers a subset of a larger archive. This spool-level policy governs whole patches failing to resolve; per-channel gaps such as uncovered geometry remain governed by the partial-coverage semantics — missing values, never errors.

Resolution and epoch boundaries are pure metadata, so attaching filters and subdivides the spool's dataframe: `len(spool)` and `get_contents()` reflect exactly what iteration will yield, and only data materializes lazily on extraction. On large archives this makes `attach_inventory` a costly one-time operation.

In inventory-backed selection, a bare track name with `None` matches channels where that track is undefined (uncovered distance is absence, never an empty-string value); actual field values use qualified names such as `coupling.coupling_type`.

Inventory-backed `select` and `unselect` operate on channels, not whole patches. Contents are trimmed to the matching channels, and when the matching region is disjoint along the fiber — a path that passes in and out of the selected coordinate range, or an undefined-coupling zone in the middle of a path — the patch is subdivided so that each contiguous matching interval becomes its own patch. Selection can therefore change both the shape and the number of patches in the spool. Optical-path validity edges work the same way along time: a fiber can break mid-recording, so a patch straddling a path epoch boundary appears in the index as its pieces, each resolving cleanly to its own window, and the data is split when extracted. `Spool.split_by_labels` (below) applies the same subdivision mechanism to annotation labels.

Acquisition boundaries are stricter: a configuration change requires stopping and restarting the acquisition, so no valid file spans one. On a straddling file `attach_inventory` raises, naming the file and the boundary; the usual fix is a correction — set the epoch time to the file boundary, the instrument's own record of the restart.

Subdivision reflects exactly what the path metadata says: a noisy geometry track can shatter what is conceptually one interval into several patches separated by small gaps. Apply `Spool.chunk` afterward to consolidate nearly-contiguous patches (`tolerance` parameter). `chunk` only merges patches with compatible attrs, so enriched fragments from different epochs will not rejoin; merging un-enriched fragments across a path epoch boundary is legal but will be re-subdivided at next resolution.

`attach_inventory` includes a parameter called `enrich`, which is `True` by default. This means each extracted patch from the spool will automatically include the applicable attrs and coords derived from the inventory. The `attrs`, `coords`, and enrich-level `on_missing` keywords pass through `attach_inventory` to that automatic enrichment.

Another useful function is `Spool.split_by_labels`. It will expand the spool to include all (or just some) of the labels. Note, with an inventory, labels are allowed to overlap. Hence, we might create a case where some of the data are included in multiple patches. It may also greatly expand the number of patches in each spool. It simply raises if no inventory is attached.

```python
labeled_spool = spool.split_by_labels(include=("hole_1", "trench_?a"), exclude=("along_fence",))
```

Each output patch carries the label it was split on as the singular `label` patch attr, so overlapping siblings remain distinguishable and later operations can select on `label` directly. The plural `labels` names the per-channel coord `enrich` can copy: singular `label` is per-patch, plural `labels` is per-channel.

### Patch operations

```python
# Enrich with all applicable attrs and coords (the default)
patch = patch.enrich(inventory)

# Or select specific attrs and coords
patch = patch.enrich(
    inventory,
    attrs=("sample_rate", "gauge_length", "interrogator.model"),
    coords=("x", "y", "z"),
    on_missing="nan",
)

# Enrich with attrs only
patch = patch.enrich(inventory, coords=False)
```

`Patch.enrich` is the single entry point for copying inventory metadata onto a patch — it resolves the full chain internally (`distance_map` or the affine map to optical distance, then the path tracks), and optical distance itself is requestable like any coord: `enrich(coords=("distance",))`. The `attrs` and `coords` keywords each accept `True` (all applicable), a tuple of names, or `False` to skip. It is the same operation `attach_inventory(enrich=True)` applies automatically to each patch extracted from the spool. The patch never retains a reference to the inventory; any operation that needs inventory context takes it as an explicit argument.

`enrich` overwrites the fields it is asked to copy; re-enriching is a refresh, not an error. Its `on_missing` governs only explicitly requested names the inventory does not define — `"raise"` (default), `"nan"` (dtype-appropriate missing marker: NaN for floats, `None` for strings), or `"skip"` (omit silently). The blanket `attrs=True`/`coords=True` forms copy what is applicable and never trigger `on_missing`. Whole-patch resolution failures belong to the spool-level policy above.

The patch resolves inventory context from its `data_source_id`, or from an explicit `data_source_id` passed to `enrich`. Because acquisition metadata is scalar per patch, `enrich` requires the patch to lie within a single acquisition and optical-path validity window and raises if it straddles a boundary — select or split the patch first.

Patches whose time axis is no longer physical (e.g., lag-time correlations) can still resolve by passing an explicit `time` argument alongside the codes, selecting the acquisition epoch and optical-path context as of that moment. `time` is accepted only when the patch has no physical time coordinate; for a patch with a real time axis, `enrich` raises — select or split instead.

```python
patch = patch.enrich(
    inventory,
    data_source_id="DAS.L001.01.RAW",
    time="2024-05-01T00:00:00",
    coords=("x", "y", "z"),
)
```

## Working with Archives
Native files carry no network, fiber-array, location, or acquisition codes, and rewriting every file to embed them is costly and format-dependent. Instead, encode the metadata in the archive layout itself using [hive-style](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/dataset.html#partitioned-datasets-multiple-files) directory names. DASCore's file scanning parses any path segment of the form `key=value` as a string patch attribute applied to every file below it. Since paths are already stored in the spool index, this adds no scanning cost, and partition-aware tools such as PyArrow, DuckDB, and polars can query the same layout directly without DASCore in the loop (assuming they know how to read the files in question).

An archive laid out this way might look like:

::: {.adhoc-tree}
<pre><code><span class="tree-folder tree-root">archive/</span>
├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-config">inventory.yaml</span>
├── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">network=DAS/</span>
│   ├── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">fiber_array=R2D1/</span>
│   │   └── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">location=01/</span>
│   │       └── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">acquisition=HHZ/</span>
│   │           ├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_000000.h5</span>
│   │           ├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_010000.h5</span>
│   │           └── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_020000.h5</span>
│   └── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">fiber_array=R2D2/</span>
│       └── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">location=01/</span>
│           └── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">acquisition=HHZ/</span>
│               ├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_000000.h5</span>
│               ├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_010000.h5</span>
│               └── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_020000.h5</span>
└── <span class="tree-folder tree-notes">field_notes/</span>
    ├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-markdown">deployment_log.md</span>
    └── <span class="tree-file tree-file-table">tap_tests.csv</span></code></pre>
:::

Files under `network=DAS/fiber_array=R2D1/location=01/acquisition=HHZ/` resolve to the data source ID `DAS.R2D1.01.HHZ`, making it simple to "bolt on" a DASDAE inventory to virtually any DFOS data archive that can be reorganized (or symlinked) into this layout.

For flatter archives, the four component keys can be collapsed into a single composite segment whose key is exactly the attr name:

::: {.adhoc-tree}
<pre><code><span class="tree-folder tree-root">archive/</span>
├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-config">inventory.yaml</span>
├── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">data_source_id=DAS.R2D1.01.HHZ/</span>
│   ├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_000000.h5</span>
│   └── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_010000.h5</span>
└── <span class="tree-folder tree-data">data_source_id=DAS.R2D2.01.HHZ/</span>
    ├── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_000000.h5</span>
    └── <span class="tree-file tree-file-data">2024-05-01_010000.h5</span></code></pre>
:::

Generic `key=value` parsing sets `data_source_id` directly — no special machinery. It is also branch-agnostic: the second token may name a fiber array or a station, and the resolver distinguishes them through the disjoint code namespaces. DASCore derives the four component attrs from the composite at scan time, so plain selections such as `spool.select(network="DAS")` work on either layout.

A few rules keep the scheme predictable:

- All four `data_source_id` parts must be present for inventory resolution. Partial keys are legal at the scanning layer and remain useful as plain attrs for `spool.select`, but missing parts are never guessed or defaulted; patches without a complete `data_source_id` have no valid inventory entry.
- Path-derived attributes are always strings. Anything richer belongs in the inventory.
- Path segments fill attributes the file does not define; they never override. If a file-embedded attribute disagrees with a path segment, scanning raises rather than applying precedence — the same treatment as composite/component disagreement below. The raise typically indicates a file moved into the wrong directory.
- Merged or derived products have no single ancestor, so there is nothing true to assert with provenance keys; store them under plain directories (path segments without `key=value` assert nothing), where their file-embedded attributes — including a cleared `data_source_id` — stand as written.
- Keys and values should stick to code-safe characters (letters, digits, `-`); `=`, `/`, and `.` are not allowed in values. A blank location code is unrepresentable in a `key=value` segment, so archives either use an explicit code (`location=00`, recommended) or the composite form, which carries blank as an empty token (`data_source_id=DAS.L001..RAW`). The composite `data_source_id` key is the one exception to the dot ban: its value must be exactly four dot-separated code-safe tokens, of which only the location may be empty.
- Composite and component keys on the same path must agree part-for-part, agree-or-raise.
- Values should be short, station-like codes. This keeps `data_source_id` readable and total path lengths well clear of the Windows 260-character default limit (deep archives on Windows may still need [long paths enabled](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/maximum-file-path-limitation)).
